steps: MKS is a system of units based on metre for length, kilogram for mass and second for time.
SI (International System of Units) is the internationally accepted system of measurement.
SI includes the MKS units and additional base units, such as ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
items.finalAnswer: MKS uses metre, kilogram and second as its basic units; SI is the international system and includes these units along with additional basic units.

steps: The five basic SI units commonly used in Chemistry are:
Length — metre (m).
Mass — kilogram (kg).
Time — second (s).
Temperature — kelvin (K).
Amount of substance — mole (mol).
items.finalAnswer: The five basic SI units commonly used in Chemistry are metre, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.

steps: Area is a derived quantity: area = length × breadth; its SI unit is square metre (m²).
Volume is a derived quantity: volume = length × breadth × height; its SI unit is cubic metre (m³).
Density is a derived quantity: density = mass ÷ volume; its SI unit is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m³).
items.finalAnswer: Area, volume and density have derived SI units: m², m³ and kg/m³, respectively.

steps: In Chemistry, the masses and volumes of substances used in the laboratory are usually small.
Using the kilogram and cubic metre for these quantities would give inconveniently small numerical values.
Therefore, smaller units such as gram (g), milligram (mg), cubic centimetre (cm³) and millilitre (mL) are more convenient.
items.finalAnswer: Smaller units are preferred because the masses and volumes commonly measured in Chemistry are small and are more conveniently expressed in units such as grams and millilitres.

steps: Using different units for the same quantity makes measurements difficult to compare.
It makes communication and the exchange of measurement results confusing.
Conversions between different units can cause mistakes and lead to incorrect results.
items.finalAnswer: Different units make measurements difficult to compare and communicate, and increase the chance of conversion errors.

steps: Traditional units of mass include tola, seer and maund.
Traditional units of volume include seer and pail.
Traditional units of length include inch, foot, yard and gaz.
items.finalAnswer: Examples of traditional units are tola, seer and maund for mass; seer and pail for volume; and inch, foot, yard and gaz for length.

steps: Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true or accepted value.
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
A measurement may be precise without being accurate, and accurate without being highly precise.
items.finalAnswer: Accuracy describes closeness to the true value, whereas precision describes closeness among repeated measurements.

steps: Use a properly calibrated instrument and check it for zero error before taking a measurement.
Use the instrument correctly and read its scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Where possible, compare the measurement with a standard instrument or reference.
items.finalAnswer: Systematic errors can be reduced by calibrating instruments, checking for zero error and using and reading the instrument correctly.
